Their landlord in Bengaluru had given notice with just three weeks to go, and Tanvir and Salma had shortlisted three flats in a hurry. On Friday night, with the packing boxes around them, Salma opened a spreadsheet: rent, size, commute, balcony, floor.
"Let's weight them," Tanvir said. They tried equal weights. Flat B won. Then Salma, who loved cooking, doubled the weight on size. Still B. Tanvir doubled rent. Still B.
Salma frowned. "Why does B always win?"
Tanvir scrolled across. "Look. B is twenty minutes from both our offices. The others are over an hour for one of us. Commute swamps everything else."
They sat quietly for a second.
"So what we actually care about," Salma said slowly, "is not being stuck in traffic every evening."
"And having dinner together," Tanvir said.
They booked B the next morning.

qa.q: How far is flat B from both offices?
qa.a: B is twenty minutes from both their offices.

qa.q: How did Salma feel on realising that commute decided every result?
qa.a: Salma was surprised and then thoughtful, realising what they truly cared about was not being stuck in traffic every evening.

qa.q: What else could Tanvir and Salma try to double-check their choice?
qa.a: They could each drive or ride the route to B at rush hour once, since commute is the criterion that decides everything.

qa.q: How might the choice look to Tanvir?
qa.a: Tanvir sees the commute swamping everything else and ties it to what matters to Tanvir, having dinner together.

grounding: It shows a young couple comparing flats and noticing that whatever the weights, commute decides the result, revealing what they care about.

Uma and Anirban had been arguing about flats for two weekends in their rented room in Kolkata. So on Sunday Anirban drew a matrix on the back of a wedding card: three flats, five criteria.
Uma scored. Anirban scored. They tried three sets of weights: hers, his, and one they agreed on.
Every time, the Behala flat lost and the Salt Lake one won.
"Wait," Uma said. "Why does Salt Lake win even with my weights? I gave space the most."
Anirban traced the numbers with a pencil. "Because Behala is an hour and a half from my office and an hour from yours. Every set of weights has commute in it, and it's killing Behala."
Uma leaned back. "So all that fighting about the balcony and the kitchen..."
"...wasn't the real thing," Anirban said. "We just hate long rides."
They both laughed.

qa.q: On what did Anirban draw the matrix?
qa.a: He drew it on the back of a wedding card.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when she leaned back after Anirban's explanation?
qa.a: She felt surprised and a bit sheepish, realising two weekends of arguing were about the wrong things.

qa.q: What else could Uma and Anirban do now that they know commute matters most?
qa.a: They could look for more flats near both offices, since the matrix showed that criterion drives the whole choice.

qa.q: How might Anirban see the matrix after this?
qa.a: Anirban sees it as a tool that ended their argument by showing what they both actually care about.

grounding: It shows a young couple finding that commute time decides the outcome whatever weights they use, which reveals what they truly care about.
